questions.question: In Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 6Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 14H<sup>+</sup> → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 6Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 7H<sub>2</sub>O, what is the mole ratio of oxidising agent to reducing agent, and which species is the oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> (reduced, Cr +6 to +3) is the oxidising agent with coefficient 1, while Fe<sup>2+</sup> (oxidised, +2 to +3) is the reducing agent with coefficient 6, giving a 1 : 6 ratio of oxidising to reducing agent.
questions.hint: Match each species to whether it is reduced or oxidised, then read off its coefficient.
distractor_logic: this reverses the ratio; Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>'s coefficient is 1, not 6, and Fe<sup>2+</sup> is the reducing agent, not oxidising
Fe<sup>2+</sup> is oxidised, making it the reducing agent, not the oxidising agent
14 is the H<sup>+</sup> coefficient, which is unrelated to the oxidising:reducing agent ratio

questions.question: At the anode of the Daniel cell, zinc's oxidation number changes from 0 to +2. How many electrons does this release per Zn atom, and where do these electrons ultimately go?
options: 2 electrons; through the external circuit to the cathode, reducing Cu<sup>2+</sup>
2 electrons; they remain on the anode
3 electrons; through the external circuit to the cathode
questions.explanation: A change from 0 to +2 requires the loss of 2 electrons per Zn atom; these electrons travel through the external circuit to the copper cathode, where they reduce Cu<sup>2+</sup> to Cu.
questions.hint: Match the oxidation-number change to the number of electrons, then recall where electrons flow in a galvanic cell.
distractor_logic: the salt bridge carries ions internally, not electrons; also, only 2 electrons are released per Zn atom, not 1
electrons must leave the anode and travel through the external circuit; they do not remain there
3 electrons would correspond to a +3 charge on zinc, but Zn only forms Zn<sup>2+</sup>

questions.question: Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>−</sup>(cold dilute) → Cl<sup>−</sup> + OCl<sup>−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O can be thought of as two half-reactions: Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → 2Cl<sup>−</sup> (reduction) and Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>−</sup> → 2OCl<sup>−</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> (oxidation, simplified). How many electrons are exchanged between these two half-reactions, and what type of redox reaction results overall?
questions.explanation: Both half-reactions involve exactly 2 electrons, allowing them to combine directly without scaling; since the same element (Cl) is both reduced and oxidised starting from Cl<sub>2</sub>, the overall reaction is a disproportionation.
questions.hint: Compare the electron count in each half-reaction — do they already match, or need scaling?
distractor_logic: the half-reactions each explicitly show 2 electrons, not 1
comproportionation is the reverse pattern (two states combining into one), not what happens here, where one state splits into two
the two half-reactions already balance at 2 electrons each; no further scaling to 4 is needed

questions.question: In the Daniel cell, zinc classically loses no oxygen or hydrogen (there is no O or H involved) yet is still said to be oxidised. Which redox concept correctly explains why Zn is called "oxidised" here, given that the classical O/H concept does not apply?
options: The classical concept always applies, even without O or H being involved
The electron-transfer concept, since Zn loses electrons to form Zn<sup>2+</sup>
Oxidation number rules do not apply to electrode processes
Zn is not actually oxidised in this cell
questions.explanation: Since no oxygen or hydrogen is involved, the classical O/H definition cannot describe this reaction; instead, the broader electron-transfer concept applies — Zn loses 2 electrons to form Zn<sup>2+</sup>, which is oxidation.
questions.hint: When O/H atoms are not involved, a more general definition of oxidation is needed.
distractor_logic: the classical O/H concept specifically requires oxygen or hydrogen transfer, which is absent here
oxidation number rules apply universally, including to electrode reactions such as this one
Zn's oxidation number clearly rises from 0 to +2, confirming it is indeed oxidised

questions.question: For MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + I<sup>−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O → MnO<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> + OH<sup>−</sup> (basic medium), Mn goes from +7 to +4 (3-electron change) and I goes from −1 to 0 (1-electron change per I atom, 2 per I<sub>2</sub> formed). What is the smallest whole-number coefficient needed for I<sup>−</sup> to balance electrons against one MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>?
questions.explanation: Each MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> gains 3 electrons; each I<sup>−</sup> loses 1 electron, so 3 I<sup>−</sup> ions are needed to supply the 3 electrons required by one MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> (giving 2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + 6I<sup>−</sup> once scaled to whole I<sub>2</sub> molecules, but the minimal I<sup>−</sup>:MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> ratio is 3:1).
questions.hint: Match the 3-electron demand of one Mn atom with enough I<sup>−</sup> ions, each supplying 1 electron.
distractor_logic: 1 I<sup>−</sup> supplies only 1 electron, not enough for Mn's 3-electron demand
2 I<sup>−</sup> ions supply only 2 electrons, still short of the 3 needed
6 would supply twice the electrons actually needed to balance one MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>

questions.question: In 2Cu<sub>2</sub>O(s) + Cu<sub>2</sub>S(s) → 6Cu(s) + SO<sub>2</sub>(g), both Cu<sub>2</sub>O and Cu<sub>2</sub>S supply Cu<sup>+</sup> that is reduced to Cu(0), while S in Cu<sub>2</sub>S is oxidised to +4. Which species should be identified as the reducing agent?
options: Cu<sub>2</sub>S, since its sulfur is oxidised
SO<sub>2</sub>, since it is the final product
Cu(s), since it is the final metal product
questions.explanation: Cu<sub>2</sub>S supplies the sulfur atom that is oxidised (−2 to +4), so Cu<sub>2</sub>S acts as the reducing agent, even though it also supplies Cu<sup>+</sup> that gets reduced — both Cu<sub>2</sub>O and Cu<sub>2</sub>S act as oxidising agents (via their Cu<sup>+</sup>), while only Cu<sub>2</sub>S additionally acts as the reducing agent (via its S<sup>2−</sup>).
questions.hint: Find which reactant contains the atom whose oxidation number rises.
distractor_logic: Cu<sub>2</sub>O contains no sulfur and does not supply the oxidised species; it acts only as an oxidising agent here
SO<sub>2</sub> is the oxidised product itself, not the reactant that supplied the electrons
Cu(s) is the reduced product, not the reactant responsible for donating electrons

questions.question: The reduction half-reaction for chromium is Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 14H<sup>+</sup> + 6e<sup>−</sup> → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 7H<sub>2</sub>O. Given that Cr starts at +6 in dichromate, confirm the oxidation number of Cr in the product, and state how many water molecules form per Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> ion reduced.
questions.explanation: The half-reaction shows the product as 2Cr<sup>3+</sup>, confirming chromium's oxidation number falls from +6 to +3, and 7 water molecules are formed per Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> ion, as balanced by the 14 H<sup>+</sup> and 7 oxygen atoms from dichromate.
questions.hint: Read the product's charge directly from the half-reaction, and count the H<sub>2</sub>O coefficient shown.
distractor_logic: Cr<sup>3+</sup> means +3, not +2; the half-reaction explicitly shows Cr<sup>3+</sup> as the product
the half-reaction explicitly shows 7 water molecules, not 14, as its coefficient
the half-reaction clearly shows Cr's oxidation number changing (via the 6 electrons), not staying at +6

questions.question: In Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) → Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + e<sup>−</sup>, Fe<sup>2+</sup> is oxidised. If this half-reaction is coupled with the reduction of Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> to Cr<sup>3+</sup> (a 6-electron process per Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>), how many Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions are needed as the reducing agent per dichromate ion reduced?
questions.explanation: Since each Fe<sup>2+</sup> supplies exactly 1 electron and Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> requires 6 electrons to be fully reduced, exactly 6 Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions are needed as the reducing agent per dichromate ion.
questions.hint: Match the 1-electron supply of each Fe<sup>2+</sup> against the 6-electron demand of one dichromate ion.
distractor_logic: 1 Fe<sup>2+</sup> supplies only 1 electron, far short of the 6 electrons Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> requires
3 Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions supply only 3 electrons, still short of the 6 needed
14 is the H<sup>+</sup> coefficient in the full balanced equation, not the Fe<sup>2+</sup> coefficient

topics.name: Classical Idea of Redox Reactions
topics.summary: Long before electrons were understood, chemists classified reactions by oxygen and hydrogen transfer. Oxidation was defined as the addition of oxygen (or an electronegative element) to a substance, or the removal of hydrogen (or an electropositive element) from it — e.g. 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. Reduction was defined as the opposite: removal of oxygen, or addition of hydrogen — e.g. CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O, where CuO is reduced (loses O) while H2 is oxidised (gains O). Because one substance's oxygen loss is always another's oxygen gain, oxidation and reduction can never occur alone — they always occur together, which is exactly why such reactions are called redox (reduction + oxidation) reactions. This classical picture works well for simple O/H-transfer reactions but breaks down for reactions with no oxygen or hydrogen at all (like Zn + Cu2+), which is why the electron-transfer concept was developed next.
key_formulas: Oxidation (classical) = addition of O / removal of H
Reduction (classical) = removal of O / addition of H
topics.worked_example: In 3Fe(s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O(g) → Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>(g), iron gains oxygen (classically oxidised) while water loses oxygen, ending up as H<sub>2</sub> (water is classically reduced).
common_mistakes: Assuming oxidation always needs oxygen to be present — many redox reactions (e.g. involving only metal ions) have no oxygen at all
Confusing which reactant is 'oxidised' versus 'reduced' by focusing on the product formed instead of tracking what each original reactant gained or lost
Forgetting that oxidation and reduction are always simultaneous, never independent, in a single reaction

topics.name: Redox Reactions in Terms of Electron Transfer
topics.summary: The electron-transfer concept generalises the classical idea to cover every redox reaction, not just O/H-transfer ones. Oxidation is the loss of one or more electrons ("LEO" — Loss of Electrons is Oxidation), and reduction is the gain of one or more electrons ("GER" — Gain of Electrons is Reduction). For example, in Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s), zinc loses 2 electrons (Zn → Zn2+ + 2e−, oxidation) while Cu2+ gains those same 2 electrons (Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu, reduction). The number of electrons lost by the species oxidised must always exactly equal the number gained by the species reduced — this electron-balance principle underlies every method of balancing redox equations. Splitting a full redox equation into two such electron half-reactions (one oxidation, one reduction) is the basis of the ion-electron balancing method.
key_formulas: Oxidation: X → X<sup>n+</sup> + ne<sup>−</sup>
Reduction: Y<sup>n+</sup> + ne<sup>−</sup> → Y
Electrons lost (by oxidised species) = Electrons gained (by reduced species)
topics.worked_example: For 2Al(s) + 3Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) → 2Al<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + 3Cu(s): each Al atom loses 3 electrons (2 × 3 = 6 total), and each Cu<sup>2+</sup> gains 2 electrons (3 × 2 = 6 total) — the two totals match exactly.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the per-atom electron change by the number of atoms actually reacting when checking the overall electron balance
Mixing up which species loses electrons (reducing agent, itself oxidised) and which gains them (oxidising agent, itself reduced)
Assuming the electron count equals the ionic charge shown, without checking the actual change from the starting oxidation state

topics.name: Oxidation Number — Rules and Calculation
topics.summary: The oxidation number is a bookkeeping charge assigned to an atom assuming all bonds are fully ionic, and it lets chemists track redox changes even in complex, largely covalent species. Key rules: a free element has oxidation number 0; a monoatomic ion's oxidation number equals its charge; O is usually −2 (except −1 in peroxides like H2O2, −1/2 in superoxides like KO2, and +2 in OF2); H is usually +1 (except −1 in metal hydrides like NaH); F is always −1. For a neutral molecule, all oxidation numbers must sum to zero; for a polyatomic ion, they must sum to the ion's charge. These two sum rules are the working tool for finding an unknown oxidation number, such as Mn in KMnO4 (+7) or Cr in Cr2O72− (+6). In some compounds (e.g. Na2S4O6, Fe3O4) the formula only yields an average oxidation number, since the real structure has that element in more than one true oxidation state — a recognised limitation of the concept.
key_formulas: Neutral molecule: ∑(oxidation numbers) = 0
Polyatomic ion: ∑(oxidation numbers) = ionic charge
O = −2 (usual); H = +1 (usual); F = −1 (always)
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply an atom's oxidation number by its subscript before summing (e.g. treating 7 oxygens as contributing −2 instead of −14 in K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>)
Applying oxygen's default −2 value blindly in peroxides, superoxides or OF<sub>2</sub>, where it is an exception
Treating a formula-derived average oxidation number (as in Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> or Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) as if every atom of that element truly holds that exact value

topics.name: Oxidising and Reducing Agents
topics.summary: An oxidising agent is the species that oxidises another substance by accepting electrons from it, and in doing so is itself reduced (its oxidation number decreases). A reducing agent is the species that reduces another substance by donating electrons to it, and is itself oxidised (its oxidation number increases). In Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s), Zn is the reducing agent (it is oxidised) and Cu2+ is the oxidising agent (it is reduced). Common strong oxidising agents include KMnO4 and K2Cr2O7, where the central atom sits at a very high oxidation number (+7 and +6) and so can only be reduced further. A special case is disproportionation: when a species containing an element at an intermediate oxidation state reacts such that the same element is simultaneously oxidised in part of the product and reduced in another part — that single species then acts as both the oxidising and the reducing agent at once, e.g. Cl2 in Cl2 + 2OH− → Cl− + OCl− + H2O.
key_formulas: Oxidising agent: itself reduced (ON decreases)
Reducing agent: itself oxidised (ON increases)
Disproportionation needs an intermediate starting oxidation state
topics.worked_example: In MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + 5Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 8H<sup>+</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 5Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O, MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> (Mn: +7→+2) is the oxidising agent and Fe<sup>2+</sup> (+2→+3) is the reducing agent.
common_mistakes: Labelling the product (e.g. Cu, Fe<sup>3+</sup>) as the oxidising or reducing agent instead of the original reactant it came from
Assuming a species at its highest possible oxidation number (e.g. Mn in KMnO<sub>4</sub>) could act as a reducing agent, when it can in fact only be reduced further
Missing that in a disproportionation reaction, one single reactant species is the answer to both 'which is the oxidising agent' and 'which is the reducing agent'

topics.name: Types of Redox Reactions
topics.summary: Redox reactions are commonly grouped into four types. Combination reactions join two or more reactants into a single product, e.g. 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. Decomposition reactions break a single compound into two or more products, e.g. 2KClO3 →Δ 2KCl + 3O2 (though not every decomposition is redox — CaCO3 →Δ CaO + CO2 involves no oxidation-number change at all). Displacement reactions occur when one element replaces another from a compound, either a metal displacing a metal (Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu) or a non-metal displacing a non-metal (Cl2 + 2KI → 2KCl + I2). Disproportionation reactions involve a single species, with an element at an intermediate oxidation state, splitting into two products where that element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, e.g. 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2. Always check oxidation numbers carefully before classifying — some reactions that look redox at first glance (like CaCO3 decomposing) involve no electron transfer at all.
key_formulas: Combination: A + B → AB
Decomposition: AB → A + B
Displacement: A + BC → AC + B
Disproportionation: one species → oxidised product + reduced product
topics.worked_example: 3Cl<sub>2</sub> + 6OH<sup>−</sup>(hot, conc.) → 5Cl<sup>−</sup> + ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O is a disproportionation: Cl (0) is reduced to −1 (Cl<sup>−</sup>) and oxidised all the way to +5 (ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>).
common_mistakes: Assuming every decomposition or every combination reaction must automatically be a redox reaction, without checking oxidation numbers
Confusing a displacement reaction (one element replacing another in a compound) with a simple combination or decomposition
Missing that reaction conditions (cold dilute vs hot concentrated base) can change which disproportionation products form, and to what oxidation state

topics.name: Balancing Redox Reactions — Oxidation Number Method
topics.summary: This method balances a redox equation using oxidation-number changes directly. Steps: (1) write the skeletal equation and assign oxidation numbers to every atom; (2) identify the atoms whose oxidation number changes, and calculate the increase or decrease per atom; (3) choose coefficients so that the total increase in oxidation number equals the total decrease (multiplying by the number of atoms involved where needed); (4) balance all other atoms; (5) balance charge by adding H+ ions in acidic medium or OH− ions in basic medium; (6) balance oxygen and hydrogen with H2O. For example, in MnO4− + Fe2+ + H+ → Mn2+ + Fe3+ + H2O, Mn drops by 5 units while each Fe rises by 1 unit, so 5 Fe2+ are needed per MnO4−, giving MnO4− + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ → Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O.
key_formulas: Total increase in oxidation number = Total decrease in oxidation number
Acidic medium: balance charge with H<sup>+</sup>
Basic medium: balance charge with OH<sup>−</sup>
topics.worked_example: For Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + Fe<sup>2+</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → Cr<sup>3+</sup> + Fe<sup>3+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O: 2 Cr atoms drop 3 units each (total 6), matched by 6 Fe<sup>2+</sup> each rising 1 unit, giving Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 6Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 14H<sup>+</sup> → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 6Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 7H<sub>2</sub>O.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the per-atom oxidation-number change by the number of that atom present in the formula (e.g. 2 Cr atoms in Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>, not 1)
Adding H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup> in the same equation, instead of choosing the one appropriate to the stated medium
Balancing H and O before finishing the electron-change balance, leading to a coefficient set that is atom-balanced but not electron-balanced

topics.name: Balancing Redox Reactions — Half-Reaction (Ion-Electron) Method
topics.summary: This method splits the equation into two half-reactions — one oxidation, one reduction — and balances each independently before combining them. Steps (acidic medium): (1) split into two half-reactions; (2) balance all atoms except O and H; (3) balance O by adding H<sub>2</sub>O; (4) balance H by adding H<sup>+</sup>; (5) balance charge by adding electrons; (6) multiply each half-reaction so both contain the same number of electrons, then add them together, cancelling electrons and any species common to both sides. For basic medium, complete the acidic-medium balance first, then add OH<sup>−</sup> equal to the H<sup>+</sup> present on both sides, combining H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup> into H<sub>2</sub>O and cancelling any repeated water. For example, the reduction half-reaction MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 5e<sup>−</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O is combined with the oxidation half-reaction Fe<sup>2+</sup> → Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>−</sup> (multiplied by 5) to give the full balanced equation.
key_formulas: Balance O with H<sub>2</sub>O, then H with H<sup>+</sup> (acidic medium)
Balance charge by adding electrons to the more positive side
Scale each half-reaction so electron counts match before adding
topics.worked_example: Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 14H<sup>+</sup> → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 7H<sub>2</sub>O has a left-side charge of +12 and a right-side charge of +6, so 6 electrons must be added to the left to balance charge: Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 14H<sup>+</sup> + 6e<sup>−</sup> → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 7H<sub>2</sub>O.
common_mistakes: Balancing electrons before atoms are fully balanced, which gives a half-reaction that looks charge-balanced but is not atom-balanced
Forgetting to scale up the *entire* half-reaction (all species, not just the electrons) when matching electron counts between the two half-reactions
Skipping the OH<sup>−</sup>-conversion step for basic medium and leaving H<sup>+</sup> in a reaction that is stated to occur in alkaline conditions

topics.name: Redox Reactions and Electrode Processes
topics.summary: Redox reactions can be physically separated into two half-cells connected by a wire and a salt bridge, forming an electrochemical (galvanic) cell that converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Oxidation always occurs at the anode, and reduction always occurs at the cathode. In the classic Daniel cell, Zn(s) | ZnSO4(aq) || CuSO4(aq) | Cu(s), zinc is oxidised at the anode (Zn → Zn2+ + 2e−) while Cu2+ is reduced at the cathode (Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu), giving the overall cell reaction Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s). Electrons released at the anode travel through the external circuit to the cathode, where they are consumed; the zinc electrode loses mass as it dissolves, while the copper electrode gains mass as copper is deposited. This electrode picture connects redox chemistry directly to the operation of batteries and other electrochemical cells, and to the standard hydrogen electrode used as the zero-point reference for electrode potentials.
key_formulas: Oxidation occurs at the anode; reduction occurs at the cathode
Electrons flow (external circuit): anode → cathode
Overall cell reaction = anode half-reaction + cathode half-reaction
topics.worked_example: In the Daniel cell, if 2 mol of electrons flow through the circuit, exactly 1 mol of Zn dissolves at the anode and exactly 1 mol of Cu is deposited at the cathode (each needing 2 electrons per atom).
common_mistakes: Mixing up anode and cathode, especially remembering which one hosts oxidation versus reduction
Thinking electrons flow through the salt bridge, when the salt bridge only carries ions to maintain electrical neutrality, while electrons travel through the external wire
Assuming both electrodes always gain or both always lose mass, instead of recognising that one electrode dissolves while the other typically gains deposited metal
